Headline: Developer Left PHP Server Unpatched With Bitcoin Inside, but Hackers Hit an Unexpected Roadblock
Sources: CCN.com, CryptoSlate, www.techtimes.co.uk
Coin in this story: Bitcoin (BTC) $80,373, +0.1% in 24h

Article text:
Bitcoin wallet Electrum has patched a security flaw that allowed hackers to redirect payments when users tried to increase transaction fees. The developers disclosed the vulnerability on Oct. 24, confirming that malicious servers had exploited the weakness and that at least one user lost Bitcoin after unknowingly approving a fraudulent transaction. The high-severity vulnerability affects Electrum versions earlier than 4.8.3. It exploits the wallet's reliance on external servers to track unconfirmed transactions, allowing attackers to manipulate the payment information users see before they authorize additional fees. The disclosure followed two complaints received on Oct. 11 and Oct. 18. The first user noticed an unfamiliar transaction appearing in their wallet after broadcasting a payment, while the second reported losing funds after attempting to accelerate a pending transfer. Both incidents involved attackers generating Bitcoin addresses that matched the final four characters of the intended recipients' addresses, potentially deceiving users who relied on partial address checks. Electrum did not disclose the amount stolen, although its maintainers confirmed that some servers were actively carrying out the attack. The exploit takes advantage of a weakness in how Electrum processes transaction information supplied by its connected servers. When a user broadcasts a Bitcoin payment, a malicious server can withhold the transaction from the network and instead supply a conflicting version that redirects the funds to an attacker-controlled address. The fraudulent transaction initially contains invalid signatures, meaning it cannot be processed as a legitimate payment. However, affected Electrum clients failed to verify those signatures before displaying the substituted transaction in the wallet's unconfirmed history. As a result, the legitimate payment disappears from that view, leaving the user with a manipulated transaction that appears to be awaiting confirmation. The attacker can then exploit Bitcoin's Replace-by-Fee feature, which allows users to increase transaction fees to encourage miners to confirm delayed payments. If the victim manually increases the fee on the substituted transaction, Electrum generates fresh signatures authorizing its altered payment details. That approval makes the attacker-directed transaction valid, allowing the funds to transfer without compromising the user's private keys. In the Oct. 18 incident, the attackers reportedly set the fraudulent transaction fee to zero, potentially encouraging the victim to raise it. The case shows how a routine wallet function can become a theft mechanism when the client accepts transaction details from an untrusted server without adequate verification. Electrum's latest release introduces signature checks for wallet-owned inputs before unconfirmed transactions enter the client's local history, preventing the reported substitution technique from reaching the fee-adjustment stage. The developers tagged version 4.8.3 on Oct. 23 and distributed the updated software on Oct. 24, alongside the public security disclosure. They advised users to download the patch from Electrum's official website and verify complete recipient addresses and payment amounts whenever signing transactions. The advisory also says clients connected exclusively to trusted servers, including privately operated ones, are not exposed to this attack. The patch does not extend signature verification to every incoming transaction. Oluwapelumi values Bitcoin's potential. Headline: OCC's final rule to start fresh in weighing stablecoin rewards against GENIUS Act ban
Sources: CoinDesk, Cointelegraph, The Block, Wu Blockchain

Telegram news posts about it:
OCC Finalizes First GENIUS Act Rule: No Safe Harbor for Existing Stablecoin Rewards

The OCC has issued its first final rule implementing the GENIUS Act, covering stablecoin issuance, custody, and third-party partnerships, effective January 18, 2027. Existing yield and rewards programs receive no automatic grandfathering or safe harbor; compliance will be assessed case by case.

The act prohibits issuers from paying yield solely for holding, using, or retaining stablecoins, but does not ban all third-party rewards. The OCC said rewards based at least partly on other factors may fall outside the prohibition. The implications for programs offered by Coinbase, PayPal, and Kraken remain uncertain. — link
🇺🇸 BREAKING: The US OCC finalizes GENIUS Act rules for stablecoin issuers, covering reserves, redemptions, and custody.

Effective January 18, 2027.

News | Markets | YouTube
Article text:
5 min readMake  preferred on ShareShare this articleCopy linkX iconX (Twitter)LinkedInFacebookEmailMake  preferred on Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould (Nikhilesh De/CoinDesk) SummaryShowThe U.S. agency that regulates national banks and trusts has issued the first final rule putting the GENIUS Act into place in January, though a number of other regulators are still working on other parts of the implementation.The section on stablecoin yield doesn't offer a lot of detail on what activity may fall under the law's wide prohibition of such yield from issuers, but the crypto industry has already interpreted GENIUS to permit the rewards programs that have become commonplace with stablecoin activity on exchanges.The final rule states that pre-existing rewards programs won't get special treatment as the OCC assesses which ones pass regulatory muster.U.S. crypto exchanges that have long been giving people rewards for usings stablecoins will have to get the agency to sign off on those existing programs, according to the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the first federal banking regulator to issue a final rule under the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act. The OCC, which oversees U.S. national banks and trusts that will play a central role in the issuance of stablecoins under the law, issued a final rule on Wednesday to establish the regulations under which the firms that issue the dollar-based tokens will operate — including in their third-party relationships with the exchanges on which their stablecoins change hands. The agency — an independent bureau of the Treasury Department — has declined to offer examples or illustrations of what type of rewards operations may run afoul of the GENIUS Act, which declared that payments to customers made "solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin" won't be allowed. The industry, which won't get any safe harbors for existing programs, will just have to test the agency's case-by-case oversight to get a better sense of the rule, which is set to go live on January 18. The regulator said it "will apply the language of the statute to the facts and circumstances of any particular arrangement." However, the agency did suggest that the word "solely" in the prohibition is carrying a lot of weight, and that a reward that "might be made, at least in part, for other reasons" would fall outside the ban in the GENIUS Act. Payment stablecoins hew to the value of the U.S. dollar and are designed — as suggested by the name — to maintain a steady value in a crypto industry in which other assets are known to be famously volatile. The sector is currently led by Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC, but a number of entrants have begun crowding into the space.
